newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt testing market for Eurobond issue in pounds.
newsitem.headline: Egypt testing market for Eurobond issue in pounds.

text.p: The Egyptian government wants to issue two-year bonds denominated in Egyptian pounds on the Eurobond or foreign bond market as a gesture to put the currency on the international map, officials said on Thursday.
It has approached international banks with a proposal to issue bonds worth one billion pounds ($290 million), a consultant in the prime minister's office told Reuters.
"We're welcoming offers at the moment," said consultant Mahmoud Mohieldin. Details of the timing and the yield have not been decided but the yield will probably be fixed, he added.
"We are testing the waters," added Youssef Boutros-Ghali, the minister of state for economic affairs.
The bond will be the first of its type traded abroad though foreign institutions have subscribed to the Egyptian treasury bonds issued in 1995 and 1996.
"Egypt is interested in seeing Europounds issued, in the same way as Czech Eurocrowns, to be put on the map, to show they are there," one official said.
Mohieldin said the government did not need the money but could use it for development projects like a plan to irrigate 500,000 acres (200,000 hectares) in the Western Desert.

The denomination will be in pounds also because Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak, mindful of Egypt's external debt problems in the 1980s, has imposed severe restrictions on borrowing from abroad in foreign currencies.
The government thinks it can convince investors that the risk is minimal that the Egyptian pound will fall in value before the bonds mature, the officials said.
The pound has been stable against the dollar for several years and has even appreciated this month on the back of very large foreign inflows into its capital markets.

The Egyptian treasury issued seven-year bonds worth four billion pounds in October 1996 with an 11 percent yield and five-year bonds worth three billion in May 1995 with a 12 percent yield. Both issues were oversubscribed.
But interest rates have declined steadily since the first issue. The average yield on treasury bills has fallen to just under 10 percent from about 10.8 percent in May 1995.
